To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) protection against experimental shigellosis in the guinea pig model can be induced by intranasal immunizations, (ii) the route and mode of immunization are critical for eliciting a protective response, and (iii) the persistence of the vaccine strains in the tissues is a critical factor in protection.

(i) intranasal immunizations with live attenuated mutants can protect guinea pigs against experimental shigellosis; (ii) this protection correlates with high local anti-lipolysaccharide (LPS) IgA levels; and (iii) intragastric vaccination with a live attenuated mutant can protect against shigellosis, but this protection does not correlate with high local anti-LPS IgA levels.

the intranasal route of immunization is not optimal for the protection of the guinea pig model of shigellosis, that the intragastric route of immunization with the purE aroc double mutant ofShigella is optimal for protection in guinea pigs, that protection does not correlate with the level of IgA in the mucosal secretions, and that persistence in the mucosa may be a key parameter of protection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the parameters that are essential for protection against experimental shigellosis.
defining the parameters underlying protection against experimental shigellosis and the development of a live attenuated vaccine against bacillary dysentry.
the development of a live attenuated Shigella vaccine that will be administered by the mucosal route, but the route of administration may be crucial to the success of this strategy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the route of immunization is a critical determinant of the protective capacity of the attenuated mutant and that, for the purE aros double mutant, the intranasal route is not suitable.
the route and the mode of administration are essential parameters for the successful use of live attenuating mutants in experimental shigellosis.
, for the protection of the mucosal surface againstShigella infection, the use of live mutants is promising but that the parameters of the protective response remain to be defined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of live, attenuated mutants in experimental models of shigellosis should be based on the following criteria: (i) a good level of protection, (ii) a low level of tissue destruction, and (iii) a long persistence of the mutant in the host.

the aroC mutation is a good candidate to attenuate virulence in Shigella spp. and to elicit a protective response, but it must be combined with another attenuating mutation, such as purE, to achieve the best protection.
protection in guinea pigs againstShigella flexnieri 5 keratoconjunctivities is best achieved by intragastric administration of a live attenuated purE aroCD mutant.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the choice of the route of immunization is crucial for protection againstShigella flexnei 5, and the use of the purE aros double mutant is a promising strategy for protection against bacillary shigellosis.
, for the Shigella spp., the use of live mutants is not a straightforward matter, since the attenuation of virulence is not always correlated with the protective capacity.
, although the use of live mutants is a promising approach to the development of a vaccine, their protective potential must be evaluated in animal models before they can be used in human trials.
